Sleath mode on. Toss in a million-token context window, multimodal input and keyboards perk up. No worries, my friend says, we got this. About six hours and a tokenizer autopsy might have unraveled the puzzle.

Space Bunny Alpha is the new nugget.

OpenRouter lists it as an anonymous third-party model with 1M context, text/image/video input and adjustable reasoning effort, currently free during the preview.

Overnight, the fingerprinting took off. Independent testing compared Space Bunny’s token counts across 50 deliberately awkward strings against hundreds of known models. Ding, ding, ding. Matches! MiniMax on all 50. Not 47. Not “similar.” Fifty out of fifty. Kimi was next at 29. That would seem to tells us MiniMax family with high confidence. MiniMax has kept the same tokenizer across multiple generations, so calling it M3.1 still requires another piece of evidence.

Enter candidate 2. Reports now say MiniMax M3.1 has appeared inside MiniMax’s own model catalog, staged but not yet whitelisted or exposed in shipping code. Do we conclude Space Bunny = MiniMax family? the evidence is strong in that one.

Reddit’s usage reports say its a “monster” for bug fixing and feature implementation; another said it handles ten subagents without collapsing in speed. But visual physics and Minecraft-style coding tests have been much weaker, sometimes clearly behind GLM-5.3. That suggests the stealth preview may be optimized more toward agentic coding throughput than pretty one-shot demos, which isn’t exactly a pressing need in corporate environments.

Back in the USA, OpenAI supplied another pretty good breadcrumb: Astra Minor is apparently real. Better than a random X screenshot because OpenAI’s own Daybreak help documentation currently references “Astra and Astra Minor” separately.

Meta has one similar-but-weaker leak. An OpenCode data page for muse-spark-1.4-contributor appeared overnight. Reddit users immediately tried to select it and mostly discovered that it doesn’t actually run yet. So Spark 1.4 looks staged somewhere in the ecosystem, but Zuck didn’t launch at Connect.

Anthropic’s next move is less mysterious: Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 are officially coming, and reports of Sonnet 5.5 partner testing are starting. I’d leave the leaked $2/$10 numbers in pencil.

Google: no meaningful Gemini 4 movement. The 3.8 Flash TTS models announced in last week’s Audio card moved to GA this week with voice design/replication and the new Voices API. Useful product rollout, but not a new-model surprise.

Tech bosses couldn’t get enough sun at the UN yesterday, they move on to China tonight. Sam Altman, Jensen Huang, Sundar Pichai, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Satya Nadella are expected to sit down at the White House with Xi Jinping. Apparently the frontier-model roadmap has moved to the dinner table.

What you’ll want to notice is who was left off the menu.

Enjoy! out.

medium.titulo: I Stopped Guessing With My Money. GPT-6 Astra Showed Me What I’d Been Missing
medium.resumo: Let me start with an uncomfortable confession.
medium.conteudo_html:
Let me start with an uncomfortable confession.

For years, I thought I was “okay” with money. Not rich, not broke, just okay. I paid my bills, I saved when I remembered to, and I told myself I’d “get serious about finances” once life calmed down.

Life never calmed down. That’s the thing nobody tells you.

What finally changed things wasn’t a get-rich-quick scheme or a guru’s course. It was something much more boring, and much more powerful: I started using GPT-6 Astra as a patient, judgment-free money partner. Not to replace my brain, but to sharpen it.

Here’s exactly what I did, and the mistakes I stopped making along the way. You can borrow every bit of it.

Mistake #1: I had no idea where my money was going

I used to say things like, “I don’t know where it all goes; it just disappears.”

Sound familiar?

So one weekend, I took a month of bank and card statements, removed anything sensitive like account numbers, and asked Astra to sort my spending into categories and tell me what stood out.

The results were humbling. Nothing was illegal or reckless. It was just hundreds of small, forgettable decisions adding up to something I’d never have chosen on purpose.

What you can do: Don’t start with a budget. Start with awareness. Look at one month of real spending before you try to change anything. You can’t fix what you’ve never actually seen.

Mistake #2: I was paying for things I’d forgotten about

Subscriptions are the quiet thieves of personal finance. A free trial here, an app I used twice there.

I asked Astra to scan my statements for recurring charges and list them with the yearly cost of each. Seeing “₹/$ X per year” next to something I hadn’t opened in months was the push I needed. I cancelled several in one sitting.

What you can do: Ask yourself about every recurring charge: “If this asked me to sign up today, would I?” If not, cancel it.

Mistake #3: I never actually understood the fine print

Loans, insurance policies, credit card terms. I used to skim, tick “I agree,” and hope for the best.

Now I paste the confusing sections in and say: “Explain this like I’m smart but new to finance. What are the catches? What should I ask before signing?”

It doesn’t replace a professional, but it helps me walk into a conversation with the right questions instead of blind trust. That alone has saved me from at least one deal that looked better than it was. [Your story here if you have one.]

What you can do: Never sign something you can’t explain back in your own words. If you can’t, keep asking until you can.

Mistake #4: I chased hype instead of understanding

We’ve all been there. A friend, a reel, or a random post says “this is the next big thing,” and suddenly you feel like you’re missing out.

Now, before I put a rupee or dollar into anything, I use Astra as a devil’s advocate. I ask:

  • “What are the strongest arguments against this?”
  • “What would have to be true for this to go wrong?”
  • “How does this compare with a boring, low-cost alternative?”

Ninety percent of the time, the hype fades after ten minutes of honest questioning. The other ten percent, I invest with my eyes open.

What you can do: Make a rule for yourself: sleep on it and argue against it before you buy into it. Good opportunities survive scrutiny. Bad ones need you to rush.

Mistake #5: I made plans I couldn’t stick to

My old budgets were fantasies. Beautiful spreadsheets built for a version of me who never eats out and never has surprise expenses.

Now I tell Astra the truth: my income, my fixed costs, my weaknesses. I ask for a plan that fits a real human. It helped me build a simple system: automate savings the day money arrives, keep a small buffer for “life happens,” and give myself a guilt-free fun budget so I don’t rebel against my own rules.

What you can do: A budget you can follow at 70% perfection beats a perfect one you abandon in week two.

Mistake #6: I never invested in myself

The biggest financial growth for me didn’t come from cutting costs. It came from increasing what I’m capable of earning.

I use Astra to learn faster: breaking down skills I want, building practice projects, reviewing my work, preparing for negotiations, and sharpening how I present myself. A better skill set is the one asset that compounds quietly for decades.

What you can do: Pick one skill tied to your income and spend 30 minutes a day on it. Use AI as a tutor, not a shortcut.

The honest part: what AI can’t do

I’d be doing you a disservice if I made this sound like magic. A few ground rules I follow:

  1. I never share sensitive details. No account numbers, passwords, or ID numbers. Ever.
  2. I double-check important things. AI can be wrong or out of date, especially on tax rules and regulations. For big decisions, I verify with official sources or a qualified professional.
  3. The decisions stay mine. Astra gives me clarity and options. It doesn’t know my fears, my family, or my dreams. I do.
  4. It’s a tool, not a strategy. The real work is showing up consistently. AI just makes that easier.

(And to be clear: I’m not a financial advisor, and this isn’t financial advice. It’s simply what worked for me.)

If you only do one thing this week

Take your last month of spending and just look at it. Ask an AI, or do it yourself with a highlighter, to show you the patterns. Don’t judge yourself. Just notice.

Almost every financial mistake I’ve made came from not looking. Once I started looking, everything else got easier.

You don’t need to be a finance expert. You need to be curious and consistent, and willing to ask the questions you’re a little embarrassed to ask.

I’m still learning, and I’d love to hear from you. What’s the one money mistake you wish you’d caught sooner? Drop it in the comments. Someone reading this needs to hear that they’re not alone.

medium.titulo: A small experiment in peer-to-peer intelligence
medium.resumo: What happened when I tried to make a team’s memory as simple as a folder in git
medium.conteudo_html:
What happened when I tried to make a team’s memory as simple as a folder in git

This did not begin as a project. It began as something I noticed during ordinary work.

Every day I write code with an AI agent. So does everyone on my team. Each of us, in our own session, on our own laptop, teaches the agent the same things about the same codebase. Where the locks live. Why the import job retries three times. Which endpoint must never be called from a controller. The agent learns it, does good work with it, and at six o’clock the session closes and the knowledge goes with it.

The next morning my colleague’s agent learns it again. So does mine.

What struck me was not that this was a problem. Plenty of people have written about that. What struck me was how small the missing piece seemed to be. Everything the agents were learning had already been said out loud, in our sessions. It was simply never written down anywhere that another person’s agent could read.

I wondered how little it would take to change that. Not a platform. Not a service with accounts and a database. Something closer to a shared notebook that lives inside the repository, that every agent on the team reads before it starts and adds to when it finishes. Knowledge passing from one developer’s agent to the next, through git, with nothing in the middle.

That is the experiment. I called it cosmos. This is what it turned into, what a day of real use taught me, and what I checked with a model that had no part in building it.

First, a question I had to answer for myself

Claude Code already has a memory. It is called auto memory. Claude writes notes for itself as it works, and reads them back at the start of the next session. So why build anything?

Because auto memory is private by design. It lives on your machine, in a folder under your home directory. It is never committed, never shared, and only Claude Code reads it. It is very good at what it does, which is remembering what you taught your agent. It has no opinion about your teammate, your teammate’s Codex, or the machine you will use next week.

If you are one developer, on one machine, using one tool, auto memory is enough and cosmos would be extra weight. I mean that.

The moment there are two of you, or two tools, or two machines, or a review checklist you keep repeating on every call, the private notebook stops being enough. That is the gap cosmos fills. And it does not compete with auto memory. It reads it: new notes Claude writes for itself are offered to the shared ledger, minus the personal ones.

The whole idea in one picture

You work with your agent as you always do. When a turn ends, cosmos quietly notes what happened: what you asked, which files changed, which commits landed. Later, in the background, the model reads back over those sessions and writes down only what the team would still want to know in six months. Not the chatter. The decisions and their reasons, the constraints, the things that were tried and rejected.

Each of those becomes one small markdown note, with the files that prove it, kept on its own git branch inside the repository.

From then on, whenever anyone’s agent is about to touch a file, it is told what the team knows about that file. When it finishes a change, it is asked the review questions before it stops. The knowledge moves from one developer’s session to the next, through the repository, with nobody in the middle.

Git is the database. There is nothing to run. The model is the Claude Code login each developer already has.

The parts, and how each one works

I kept the parts few and gave each a plain name. The console draws how each one works as a row of steps, and I have reproduced those drawings here.

Ledger

The Ledger is the notebook. One note per fact: a decision and its reason, a constraint, the root cause of a bug. Every note says which files prove it, when it was seen, by whom, and when it stopped being true if it did. An agent is shown one line per fact with a reference. If it wants the full note, it asks for it.

Charter

The Charter is the short page of rules the team agrees on. How we write, how we test, how we point at code, how we review our own work. It is changed in pull requests like anything else, and every agent reads it first. A rule a person wrote always outranks a habit an agent picked up.

Atlas

The Atlas is the map. It is drawn from what the repository already says about itself: package files, compose files, Kubernetes, Terraform, the API spec. It keeps a fingerprint of every file it read. When the code moves and the map does not, it says so at the start of the next session. Every service and app it finds also gets its own page, linked to the facts about that code.

Lanes

Lanes sort everything by feature, in the words a product person would use. Payments. Onboarding. Search. Each lane is a page that links its facts, its open findings, the features being planned in it, the services whose code it touches, and the people who have worked there this month. Two people drifting into the same lane is visible before it becomes a merge conflict.

Horizon

Horizon is for the moment before a feature begins. You describe it in a sentence. cosmos tells you which lanes it touches, which past decisions it collides with, which open findings are in the way, and who already knows that corner of the code. The note sits beside the code and travels with the pull request.

Gate

The Gate is the review conversation, held once, by the machine. When an agent says it is finished, it is asked whether the tests ran, where exactly the change is, whether the open findings on those files were dealt with, and what it learned that the team should keep. A one-line fix only has to say where it is. Edits to documentation are never held.

Flares

Flares are the findings QA raises. Each has a life: open, claimed, in a pull request, fixed. A fixed bug that comes back is marked as a regression. A commit message that names a flare closes it. A flare left open for two weeks becomes a decision for a person rather than a line in a document nobody reopens.

Dreams

Dreams are the background work, and they start by themselves. When enough has gathered, the model reads the recent sessions, the git history, the pull-request review comments and each developer’s own private notes. It keeps what matters, merges duplicates, notices contradictions, checks doubtful facts against today’s code, and measures how well it can find its own facts again.

Verdicts

Verdicts is where a person decides. Two facts that disagree. A fact whose evidence has gone. A finding nobody closed. cosmos does not guess on these. It shows the evidence side by side and waits. The decision, with a name and a date, becomes part of the memory too.

The details that turned out to matter

A few decisions were small to make and large in effect. I want to record them, because they are the kind of thing that only shows up after real use.

The memory has its own branch. For a while the notes lived in a folder committed alongside the code, and every feature branch picked up memory changes it had nothing to do with. People had to keep policing them out of their commits. Now the folder is a git worktree of a branch named cosmos, ignored by every other branch. The dreams commit and push it themselves. A fresh clone attaches it on its first session start.

A doubtful fact is never shown to an agent. When a fact names an identifier that has disappeared from the code, or its evidence file is gone from every branch, it stops being handed out as knowledge. It goes to a person, or to the model with today’s code in front of it. This one came from the agent’s own review, which I will get to.

Every turn leaves a journal line. Facts are what the team learned. The journal is what the team did: one line per agent turn with the ask, the files, the commits. A session that ships five commits and teaches no new fact is still on record. The git history feeds the same journal, so teammates who never installed anything appear in it from their commits alone.

The last thing said on a branch is its handoff. The agent’s final message on an editing turn is kept per branch. The next session on that branch, on any machine, opens with it. Nobody writes a second summary.

The format is not mine. Google published an open specification in June 2026 called the Open Knowledge Format: knowledge as a folder of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, with fields for provenance, trust and freshness. The cosmos ledger was already that shape, so I made it conform rather than keep my own names. Every note now carries a type, who generated it, who verified it, when it goes stale, and links to its lane and to the notes it supersedes or contradicts. Any tool that reads the format can read a cosmos ledger, and I did not have to invent a relationship model. Standard markdown links do the job.

Search is BM25, not vectors. I replaced a token-overlap ranking with the classic BM25 formula, with extra weight on matches against a fact’s evidence paths. On a real ledger of 279 test cases, the right fact reached the top five 84 percent of the time instead of 73. No embeddings, no database, forty lines of standard-library Python.

What a day of real use taught me

I tried cosmos on a real backend with about a dozen people committing to it. At the end of the day I did something I now recommend to anyone building for agents: I asked the agent that had worked inside it all day to tell me honestly what it thought.

It was the most useful review I received, and it did not hold back.

It said a stale fact shown with confidence is worse than no fact, because it would cite it. It was right, and that is where the freshness rules above came from.

It said a one-line fix and a five-hundred-line feature were paying the same price at the Gate. Now small changes only have to say where they are.

It said my tool had refused its fact three times with the words “too short”, when the real mistake was a wrong field name. Now the tool says which field it needs and shows an example.

It said the memory folder kept getting mixed into feature branches. That is why the memory has its own branch.

It said filing a finding was free but closing one had no ritual, so they piled up. Now they age into decisions.

Some numbers from that period, for those who like them. The model read about fifteen hundred turns of old sessions and kept a few hundred facts. Most of the facts it later doubted turned out to be false alarms from wrong file paths and from evidence that lived on another branch; nine were real and went to a person. Reading the git history and the review comments brought fourteen teammates into the picture without any of them installing anything. And a bug I would not have found otherwise: heuristic passes had quietly overwritten the lanes the model had chosen, leaving four hundred facts in a lane called “general”. Building the lane pages made it visible; fixing it took an afternoon.

Checked by something that is not Claude

There is an obvious weakness in all of the above. Claude built cosmos, and left alone, Claude would grade it. That is not a check.

So I wrote a validation harness that uses a different kind of model as the judge. Jev, from TypeSafe AI, does not write text at all. You hand it a state and a closed question, and it returns a choice, a score or a yes-or-no with a probability. It cannot flatter, and it cannot dress an answer up in prose.

The harness asks Jev seven kinds of question about what cosmos actually produced in a repository: does the cited code support this fact, should this observation have been kept, is this doubtful fact really outdated, is this retrieved fact relevant to the task, could a colleague continue from this handoff, does the journal line match the turn, and, for thirty documented claims about how cosmos works, does the source code implement the claim.

I ran the last suite against the public cosmos source. The first pass, with code excerpts cut around matching lines, confirmed eighteen claims with confidence and left twelve unconfirmed. I fed the judge whole functions instead of fragments and ran the twelve again. Twenty-nine of thirty came back implemented, twenty-five of them at high confidence. One stayed doubtful at low confidence: a piece of logic that captured a list before mutating it, which is exactly the kind of indirection the judge’s own documentation says it handles badly. The logic had a passing unit test. I rewrote it to be literal anyway, because code a judge cannot follow is code a colleague will struggle with too.

The whole exercise cost less than a cent. The harness and the report are in the repository, and anyone can run it against their own ledger.

What I left out, on purpose

There is no vector database, no hosted memory service, no knowledge graph engine, no score that grows every time a fact is shown whether or not anyone used it, and no web server listening on the network.

Other tools do those things, and some do them very well. Each needs something to run, pay for or secure. The experiment was to see how far you could get without any of that, so that the second person on the team does nothing but clone the repository.

Where the ideas came from

Little of this is original, and I would rather say so. Letta showed that git is a good home for an agent’s memory. claude-mem showed that giving an agent short titles first, and detail on request, beats filling its context. Zep showed that a fact should know when it became true and when it stopped. agentsmd showed that instruction files should be checked against the repository they describe. Unblocked showed how much of what a team knows lives in old pull requests and review threads. Google’s Open Knowledge Format gave the notes a shape other tools can read. Karpathy’s idea of an LLM wiki, a living document the model maintains instead of a pile it searches, is underneath all of it.

cosmos borrows those ideas and keeps the parts that work with nothing more than git and a command line.

If you want to try it

pip install cosmos-dev && cosmos init

That is the only command. It wires the hooks, writes the instruction files for every agent, reads the sessions your repository already had, and starts the first dream and the watcher in the background. Everyone else clones the repository and opens their agent.

The code is open source under the MIT licence at https://github.com/BiswajitBiswa/cosmos. The site, with each feature explained in plain English, is at https://biswajitbiswa.github.io/cosmos/.

If you try it, I would like to hear what broke more than what worked. It is an experiment, and that is how experiments get better.

medium.titulo: Build Beautiful Data Tables in Laravel Without the Headache
medium.resumo: Meet Zonvoir Table — a Laravel-first approach to building powerful, feature-rich data tables with Inertia and Vue.
medium.conteudo_html:
Meet Zonvoir Table — a Laravel-first approach to building powerful, feature-rich data tables with Inertia and Vue.

If you’ve built enough Laravel applications, you’ve probably faced this before. You need a simple table to display users, orders, products, employees, or transactions. At first, it sounds easy. Display the records. Add pagination. Done. Then the requirements start coming in. Search. Sorting. Row selection. Bulk actions. Sticky columns. Column visibility. Exports. Confirmation dialogs. Responsive behavior. And suddenly, your “simple table” isn’t simple anymore. That’s exactly why I built Zonvoir Table.

The Problem With Building Tables Again and Again

Data tables are everywhere in modern web applications. Admin panels, CRMs, SaaS dashboards, internal tools — almost all of them need tables. And while Laravel makes working with data incredibly productive, building the complete table experience usually requires connecting a lot of pieces yourself. You write the Eloquent query. Then pagination. Then search logic. Then sorting. Then frontend state. Then Vue components. Then actions. Then selection logic. And the next project? You build most of it again. I wanted a better approach.

Meet Zonvoir Table

Zonvoir Table is a Laravel package designed for building modern data tables with Laravel, Inertia, and Vue. The idea is simple:

Define your table in Laravel. Let Zonvoir Table handle the repetitive infrastructure. Instead of scattering table behavior across controllers and frontend components, you can describe your table through a clean PHP API. For example:
class UsersTable extends Table
{
    public function columns(): array
    {
        return [
            TextColumn::make('name')
                ->searchable()
                ->sortable(),
            TextColumn::make('email')
                ->searchable(),
            DateTimeColumn::make('created_at')
                ->sortable(),
        ];
    }
}

Then pass your table to your Inertia page:

return inertia('Users', [
    'users' => UsersTable::make(),
]);

Your table definition stays where it belongs: close to your Laravel application.

Beautiful Tables Without Sacrificing Developer Experience

A table shouldn’t only work well. It should feel good to use. Zonvoir Table is designed to give you a polished table experience while keeping the developer-facing API simple. You can build tables with features such as:

  • Searching
  • Sorting
  • Pagination
  • Row selection
  • Bulk actions
  • Row actions
  • Sticky headers and columns
  • Toggleable columns
  • Row links
  • Confirmation dialogs
  • Multiple column types
  • Data exports
  • Empty states
  • Multiple independent tables on the same page And you don’t have to rebuild the underlying infrastructure every time.

Declarative Columns

Different data deserves different presentation. Instead of filling your Vue templates with formatting conditions, Zonvoir Table provides dedicated column types.

return [
    TextColumn::make('name'),
    BadgeColumn::make('status'),
    BooleanColumn::make('active'),
    DateColumn::make('joined_at'),
    NumericColumn::make('salary'),
    ImageColumn::make('avatar'),
];

Your table definition becomes much easier to understand at a glance. The goal is for another developer to open the table class and immediately understand what the table does.

Actions Without Rebuilding the UI

Tables frequently need actions. Edit a user. Archive an order. Deactivate an employee. Delete several records. Instead of creating separate frontend infrastructure for every action, actions can be part of the table definition itself. They can support confirmation flows, styling, icons, row-level behavior, and bulk operations. That means less duplicated frontend code and a more consistent experience throughout your application.

Multiple Tables on the Same Page

Sometimes one table isn’t enough. A dashboard might contain users, orders, invoices, or other datasets simultaneously. Zonvoir Table supports independent table namespaces, allowing each table to maintain its own state. Your URL can represent something like:

?users[page]=2&users[sort]=name&orders[page]=3

Changing one table doesn’t have to reset another. It’s a small detail that becomes very important when building real applications.

Laravel First

One of the most important goals behind Zonvoir Table is keeping the package familiar to Laravel developers. It isn’t trying to replace Laravel’s way of doing things. It builds on it. Your queries remain Eloquent queries. Your configuration remains PHP. Your application remains Laravel. Inertia handles the bridge between backend and frontend, while Vue handles the interactive table experience. The result is a clean separation:

Laravel
   ↓
Table Definition
   ↓
Query + Columns + Actions
   ↓
Inertia
   ↓
Vue
   ↓
Beautiful Interactive Table

Less Table Code. More Product Code.

Every hour spent rebuilding pagination, selection logic, dropdowns, action handling, and table state is an hour that could have been spent building the actual product. That’s ultimately the reason Zonvoir Table exists. Not because tables are impossible to build. They’re not. But because we shouldn’t have to keep solving the same problem in every Laravel application.

I’m Still Building

Zonvoir Table is actively evolving. I’m focused on making it a powerful but clean table solution for the Laravel ecosystem — with a strong developer experience on the backend and a polished experience on the frontend. There’s much more planned as the package continues to grow. If you’re building with Laravel + Inertia + Vue, I’d love for you to try it. Feedback, bug reports, ideas, and contributions are welcome.

Build Your Next Table Differently

The next time your application needs a data table, you don’t have to start from scratch. Define your columns. Configure the behavior. Let the package handle the repetitive parts. And get back to building your application. Zonvoir Table Tables for Laravel, done right.

medium.titulo: The Problem with vue-i18n and Why Intlayer Fixes It
medium.resumo: When building internationalized apps with Vue 3 or Nuxt, `vue-i18n` has long been the automatic default. Kazupon and the community built a…
medium.conteudo_html:
When building internationalized apps with Vue 3 or Nuxt, `vue-i18n` has long been the automatic default. Kazupon and the community built a mature, feature-rich ecosystem, and for years it was the go-to standard for localizing Vue applications.

To understand why `vue-i18n` behaves the way it does, look at when its architecture was designed: it was conceived for the classic Single Page Application (SPA) era, back before dynamic imports (`import()`) and route-level code splitting were widely supported. In that paradigm, loading a single, monolithic translation object into memory at startup made complete sense.

However, modern frontend development is centered around aggressive page-size optimization, whether you’re leveraging Nuxt, static site generation (SSG), or fine-grained dynamic page loading. In this modern context, that centralized, global provider model has become a severe architectural bottleneck.

The primary issue isn’t just the initial runtime weight, though `@intlify/core-base` and the message compiler add around 24.3 KB gzipped before rendering any text. The real bottleneck is massive copy leakage across routes.

In typical Vue apps, `createI18n({ messages })` instantiates a global message tree containing every translation key for every supported language. The moment a user visits a simple `/contact` page, the browser is forced to download strings for `/dashboard`, `/pricing`, `/settings`, and the rest of the application. In our benchmarks on a standard 10-route, 10-locale Vite + Vue 3 app, 90% of the translation payload downloaded on a given page belonged to completely unrelated routes. Because `useI18n()` binds components to this global instance, compiling a single component in isolation dragged in an average of 200 KB of JavaScript.

Furthermore, because `t(“key.path”)` relies on dynamic runtime string evaluation, bundlers like Vite and Rollup cannot statically trace which keys are actually used. Unused translations cannot be tree-shaken, and key typos silently fail at runtime instead of being caught by TypeScript at build time.

How does Intlayer fix this?

Intlayer solves this by connecting content directly to its related components through build-time transformations rather than relying on a bloated runtime provider.

1. Direct component-to-content binding

Instead of dumping all strings into monolithic `locales/en.json` files, Intlayer collocates dictionaries directly next to the components that consume them (e.g., `Footer.content.ts` next to `Footer.vue`). As a result, components that are not imported never load unused content. Dead code and unrendered components carry zero translation weight.

2. Zero-waterfall dynamic loading with Vite

Even more powerfully, Intlayer leverages Vite’s advanced module transformations. Even when using dynamic page loading and code splitting, Intlayer attaches only the localized content consumed in that specific chunk directly into the bundle. There are no extra network requests or waterfalls awaiting remote JSON dictionaries before rendering, the component and its exact localized strings arrive together in a single chunk.

3. Strict compile-time safety

Intlayer generates strict TypeScript definitions directly from your content declarations. You get IDE autocompletion for keys and immediate build-time errors for missing translations or typos, eliminating runtime fallback surprises in production.

4. 0% leakage and 3x smaller bundles

At build time, the Intlayer compiler statically analyzes call sites and splits dictionaries so each route only downloads the strings it actually renders. In our benchmarks, page copy leakage dropped from 90% down to 0%, cutting per-page JavaScript from 134.9 KB to 47.0 KB gzipped (for reference, the baseline app without any i18n weighs 41.3 KB).

5. Drop-in migration via `@intlayer/vue-i18n`

If you have an existing Vue codebase, you don’t need to rewrite your components. The `@intlayer/vue-i18n` compat adapter exposes the exact same `vue-i18n` API (`useI18n`, `t()`, `d()`, `n()`, `$t`, `v-t`). By adding the Vite plugin and dropping the monolithic `messages` import, your existing `t(“key”)` calls automatically bind to compiled, split dictionaries — shrinking your runtime 3x and your components 23x with zero `.vue` file edits.

If you are running a localized Vue or Nuxt app in production, check your browser’s Network tab on any subpage: you will likely find that most of your downloaded JavaScript is translation copy users will never read.

Read the complete breakdown, benchmarks, and migration guides here:

- https://intlayer.org/blog/vue-i18n-vs-intlayer

- https://intlayer.org/blog/vue-i18n-vs-intlayer-vue-i18n

A Muralha Marathon anuncia sua 10ª edição, enquanto a nova Maratona de Pernambuco revela um percurso inédito. A Expo da Maratona de Salvador começa…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 24 de setembro de 2026

Mais uma vez, a desinformação de que “corrida faz tudo cair” ganhou força. A nova onda, que remete à fala da atriz Cláudia Raia, agora conta com a fisiculturista Priscila Santana e a apresentadora Cacau Colucci, do programa “Café com a Cacau”. No vídeo, elas afirmam que mulheres não devem correr para não ficarem com “bunda, peito e rosto caídos”. Diante disso, o especialista em fisiologia do exercício, Santiago, publicou um vídeo rebatendo as alegações. Respeitosamente, ele questionou a lógica de que a gravidade só afetaria quem pratica corrida e não outros exercícios, como a musculação. Santiago explicou que a corrida, um exercício aeróbico, é uma das principais ferramentas para potencializar a densidade e a biogênese mitocondrial, além de melhorar a capacidade cardiovascular, que é um dos principais preditores de longevidade. Ele reforçou que a melhor estratégia para viver mais e melhor é o treino combinado, unindo força e aeróbico, já que um melhora o outro. Sobre a pele, ele esclareceu que o problema não é a corrida, mas a falta de protetor solar e uma alimentação inadequada.

Inscrições para A Muralha Marathon 2027 abrem em breve

As inscrições para a 10ª edição de A Muralha Up and Down Marathon abrirão em lote único no dia 6 de outubro de 2026, às 19:42:19. A prova, que acontecerá no dia 15 de agosto de 2027, é conhecida por ser a única maratona no Brasil com apenas a distância de 42,195 km e por alternar seu percurso anualmente: em um ano, o trajeto sobe de Penedo para Visconde de Mauá, e no ano seguinte, desce. Por ser a décima edição, será um evento especial, e os atletas que completarem dez edições consecutivas receberão um número de peito eterno.

Netshoes é a nova patrocinadora da São Silvestre

A Netshoes foi anunciada como a nova patrocinadora da Corrida Internacional de São Silvestre. A empresa fechou um contrato de três anos e será responsável pela operação da loja oficial da prova e pela comercialização dos produtos licenciados. A notícia é positiva, mas ainda não há informações sobre a abertura das inscrições para a corrida. A demora preocupa corredores de todo o Brasil e do exterior, que precisam de tempo para programar a viagem, comprar passagens e reservar hotéis, já que os preços tendem a subir quanto mais perto da data do evento.

Pernambuco terá nova maratona com percurso inédito em 2027

Uma nova prova chega ao calendário de corridas do Brasil: a Maratona Internacional de Pernambuco. O evento está marcado para os dias 4 e 5 de setembro de 2027, com provas de 5 km e 10 km no sábado, e de 21 km e 42 km no domingo. A organização é da Federação Pernambucana de Esportes (FEPE). O percurso da maratona será inédito, com largada no Parque Santana, passando por Olinda, retornando ao Recife, cruzando a Ilha do Recife (passando pelo Forte do Brum e Marco Zero), seguindo para Boa Viagem e terminando no Parque Dona Lindu. As pré-inscrições já estão abertas e podem ser feitas através deste link.

Começa hoje a Expo da Maratona de Salvador

Começa hoje a entrega de kits para a Maratona de Salvador, sétima etapa do Circuito Brasil Gigante. A “Loja Maratona Salvador”, localizada no Shopping da Bahia, funcionará das 9h às 21h. O estande do Brasil Gigante estará presente no local, onde será possível adquirir a pulseira e as chapinhas do circuito, além de carimbar o passaporte para quem for correr a maratona. Eu estarei por lá na parte da manhã, até por volta das 14h, para conversar com os corredores e registrar suas histórias nesta jornada. Apareça para dar um oi!
